newsitem.title: USA: AMR, pilots back at table, with new airline offer.
newsitem.headline: AMR, pilots back at table, with new airline offer.

text.p: American Airlines made a new wage proposal Wednesday as it resumed contract negotiations with its pilots in advance of a weekend strike deadline.
An official of the nation's second-biggest airline, a unit of AMR Corp., said the new proposal increased the carrier's pay offer to a 6 percent raise over four years, up from 5 percent previously.
The Allied Pilots Association has asked for an 11.5 percent increase.
The airline official said the new proposal also dropped one of two stock options offered to the pilots, but retained the other, although at a $10 discount.

The official said the offer was designed to meet an apparent goal of the pilots -- additional wages rather than later income through stock -- but would also allow American Airlines to remain competitive.
There was no immediate response from the pilots, who have threatened to strike the airline at midnight Friday.

A federal mediator said during a bargaining break Tuesday that he remained hopeful a settlement could be reached to avert a strike, which would disrupt travel for some 200,000 passengers the carrier flies daily on its 2,200 routes worldwide.
Representatives of the two sides reached a tentative accord last September, but the pilots' rank-and-file rejected it in December, leading to the strike deadline and the federally mediated bagaining.
Aside from pay, also at issue is American's plan for its regional carrier, American Eagle, to use jets flown by lower-paid members of another union.
American has said it needs the jets flown by lower-paid pilots to remain competitive with other major U.S. carriers that are increasingly dropping turboprop craft for small jets on commuter services.
American has said a strike would force the unpaid furlough of most of its 90,000 American and American Eagle workers, and cost the company up to $50 million a day.
That would have a significant impact on a number of cities, including American's home base of Dallas-Forth Worth and its hubs in Chicago, Miami, New York, Los Angeles and San Juan, Puerto Rico.
Federal mediators stepped into the talks after union members rejected the tentative agreement and later negotiations failed to bridge the management-union gap.

American says its pilots are among the highest paid in the industry and that new demands would cripple its ability to compete, threatening its growth and a $6.5 billion order for up to 103 jetliners from Boeing Co.
Union leaders point to the company's announcement last month that it ran up record profits of $1.02 billion last year.

The Senate aviation subcommitee has urged President Clinton to help mediate the dispute, but the White House said it would not act unless asked by both sides, although it was closely monitoring the negotiations.
Four senators planned Wednesday to go to the White House to express concerns about the disruptions a strike would cause.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Sens. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., Bob Graham, D-Fla., Kay Bailey Hutchinson, R-Texas, and Barbara Boxer, D-Calif., were to meet White House chief of staff Erskine Bowles in the afternoon.
They are from states that serve as hubs for American Airlines.
AMR's stock gained $1 to $80.75 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
